results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response:
The major subdivisions of the Drosophila [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004952 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database. 

VFB holds extensive data related to the mushroom body, including [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004952,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body, [176](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004952,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of mushroom body") parts of the mushroom body, and [22137](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004952,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in mushroom body") images of neurons with some part in the mushroom body, among other data.

results.title: Neuron type classification
results.question: What types of Kenyon cells exist in the adult Drosophila brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains several types of Kenyon cells, including alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells, which are further subdivided into subtypes. Specifically, gamma Kenyon cells are known to exist in the adult Drosophila brain. This information comes from the VFB database, which provides neuron taxonomy information, including the classification of Kenyon cells into different types and subtypes, as referenced in VFB. Additionally, VFB holds various data related to gamma Kenyon cells, such as images, subclasses, expression patterns, scRNAseq data, and transgene expression data, with [3](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00100247,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of gamma Kenyon cell") available images, [10](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00100247,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of gamma Kenyon cell") subclasses, [23](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00100247,ExpressionOverlapsHere "Run in VFB: Expression patterns overlapping gamma Kenyon cell") overlapping expression patterns, [6](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00100247,anatScRNAseqQuery "Run in VFB: scRNAseq data for gamma Kenyon cell") scRNAseq datasets, and 23 transgene expression records.

results.title: Gene expression
results.question: What neurotransmitter do mushroom body Kenyon cells use?
results.response: The primary neurotransmitter used by [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") Kenyon cells is acetylcholine. This information comes from VFB neurotransmitter tags, which support [Kenyon cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003686 "Open Kenyon cell in Virtual Fly Brain") as cholinergic, i.e. using acetylcholine, as found using the VFB query.

results.title: Neuroanatomy
results.question: What brain regions does the antennal lobe connect to?
results.response: The [antennal lobe](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe in Virtual Fly Brain") connects to the mushroom body and lateral horn. Specifically, the antennal lobe projection neuron sends synaptic output to the mushroom body calyx and/or lateral horn. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database, which summarizes region connections. Additionally, VFB holds data on the [antennal lobe commissural pioneer interneuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00003924 "Open antennal lobe commissural pioneer interneuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), although its specific connections are not detailed in the provided evidence. According to the literature, as summarized in VFB, the antennal lobe is connected to higher brain centers via its projection neurons.

results.title: Cell count
results.question: Approximately how many neurons are in the adult Drosophila central brain?
results.response: The adult Drosophila central brain contains approximately more than 125,000 neurons, according to the Virtual Fly Brain database, as determined by the VFB query. Additionally, VFB holds data on the [adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047885 "Open adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell in Virtual Fly Brain"), including [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047885,SubclassesOf "Run in VFB: Subclasses of adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell") subclasses and [3](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00047885,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in adult central brain astrocyte-like glial cell") instances of transgene expression.

results.title: Central complex structure
results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
The main components of the [adult central complex](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004913 "Open adult central complex in Virtual Fly Brain") include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the three paired noduli, the asymmetrical bodies, and the protocerebral bridge (vfb). These components are associated with various functions, although the specific functions are not detailed in the available evidence. 

VFB holds extensive data on the adult central complex, including [1](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004913,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of adult central complex") image, [363](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004913,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in adult central complex") neurons with some part in the adult central complex, and [68](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004913,PartsOf "Run in VFB: Parts of adult central complex") parts of the adult central complex. Additionally, there are [12](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004913,TractsNervesInnervatingHere "Run in VFB: Tracts/nerves innervating adult central complex") tracts/nerves innervating the adult central complex, [16](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004913,LineageClonesIn "Run in VFB: Lineage clones found in adult central complex") lineage clones found in the adult central complex, and [86](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004913,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in adult central complex") instances of transgene expression in the adult central complex. Furthermore, VFB contains [13,781](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004913,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in adult central complex") images of neurons with some part in the adult central complex. 

The literature, such as the work by Wolff et al. (2015) and other studies, may provide more information on the functions associated with the adult central complex and its components. However, based on the provided evidence, the specific functions of the main components of the adult central complex are not specified.

results.title: Circuit motif
results.question: Describe the dopaminergic input to mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). Which DAN types connect to which MBON types?
results.response: The dopaminergic input to [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00111634 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") output neurons (MBONs) comes from various types of dopaminergic neurons. According to the literature, dopaminergic input to MBONs comes from specific DAN types, including dopaminergic PPL1 neurons and dopaminergic PAM neurons. VFB found 77 upstream class-connectivity partners matching "dopaminergic neuron" for MBON, with top mapped pairs including adult dopaminergic mushroom body input neuron to adult [mushroom body output neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00047953 "Open mushroom body output neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), as well as connections involving dopaminergic PPL1 neurons and dopaminergic PAM neurons such as dopaminergic PAM neuron 6 and dopaminergic PAM neuron 8. VFB holds extensive data on the mushroom body, including [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00111634,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body, [599](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00111634,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in mushroom body") neurons with synaptic terminals in the mushroom body, and [22137](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00111634,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in mushroom body") images of neurons with some part in the mushroom body.

results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type has an ID of [1813403998](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open 1813403998 in Virtual Fly Brain"). It is a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron, with a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer. The dendritic arbor extends outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer. LPLC2 is involved in detecting looming stimuli and is thought to play a role in eliciting a jump escape response. In terms of connections, LPLC2 is known to connect to various neurons, including adult cholinergic neurons, T5c neurons, and transmedullary neurons. This information comes from the Virtual Fly Brain database, which summarizes neuron profiles and provides term information, as well as from publications by Wu et al. (2016) and Klapoetke et al. (2017).

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain"), also referred to as [DNp01](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open DNp01 in Virtual Fly Brain"), is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior (Thomas and Wyman, 1984). Its distinct anatomy and connectivity set it apart from other neurons. The giant fiber neuron has a large descending axon and arborizes in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center. Additionally, it has dendritic arborization in the posterior ventrolateral protocerebrum and gorget (Kamikouchi et al., 2009; Matsuo et al., 2016; Namiki et al., 2018). The neuron's large cell body is located posterior to the lower protocerebrum (Koto et al., 1981), and its axon enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle (Ito et al., 2014), descending on the ipsilateral side (Koto et al., 1981; Namiki et al., 2018). 

In terms of connectivity, the giant fiber neuron receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons (Kim et al., 2020) and forms electrical synapses with downstream motor and premotor neurons at the inframedial bridge and at the axonal lateral bend (King and Wyman, 1980). VFB holds extensive data on the downstream and upstream connectivity classes for DNp01, with [361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") and [435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") records, respectively. 

For researchers interested in studying the giant fiber neuron, VFB has [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") available images of DNp01, as well as data on transgene expression in DNp01, with [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records. Relevant publications that provide more information on the giant fiber neuron include those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), and Kim et al. (2020), among others. 

Overall, the giant fiber neuron's unique anatomy, connectivity, and role in jump escape behavior make it an important area of study in Drosophila neuroscience.
